Clinical Reference · Acute Aortic Syndrome

Aortic Dissection

On this page
A tear in the aortic intima lets pulsatile blood split the media into a false lumen — a time-critical emergency where the anatomy (ascending = Type A vs descending = Type B) decides whether the patient goes to the OR in minutes or to the ICU for anti-impulse therapy.
Stanford A (ascending) vs B (distal to L subclavian) Anchor Rx: HR 60–80 · SBP <120 · β-blocker FIRST Sudden max-at-onset tearing chest/back pain Untreated Type A ≈ 1–2%/hr early; medical mortality ~58% Type A = emergent surgery
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

The aortic wall is three layers: a delicate inner intima, a thick load-bearing media of elastic laminae and smooth muscle, and an outer adventitia. Dissection begins when an intimal tear lets blood — driven at systemic pressure — burrow into the media and split it longitudinally into a false lumen alongside the original true lumen. The substrate that lets this happen is cystic medial degeneration: loss of elastic-fiber and smooth-muscle integrity from chronic hypertension, aging, or a connective-tissue gene defect (FBN1, TGFBR1/2, COL3A1). Hypertension supplies the shear; a weak media supplies the plane of cleavage.

Once started, the false lumen propagates — antegrade or retrograde — with every heartbeat. What determines how fast and how far it peels is not the peak blood pressure alone but dP/dt: the force and velocity of each ventricular ejection multiplied by how often it hits (heart rate). This single fact is the physiologic key to the entire treatment plan — we lower dP/dt first, pressure second.

delaminating plywood or a tire tread separating. The glue between the layers has failed, and each systolic pulse acts like a wedge hammered into the seam. It's not just how hard you push the wedge (blood pressure) — it's how sharply and how often you strike it (dP/dt and heart rate). Slow the strikes and soften the blow, and the layers stop peeling. That's why a β-blocker — which blunts the force and rate of each beat — comes before any pure vasodilator.
Pathophysiology of aortic dissection: an intimal tear lets pulsatile blood split the weakened media into a false lumen; dP/dt drives propagation (the anti-impulse target), and where it extends decides the syndrome.
Every therapy in this guide maps onto one step above. β-blockers / non-DHP CCBs cut dP/dt (force × rate) — the propagation engine — and so they go first. Vasodilators (nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroprusside) then bring peak wall stress down by lowering SBP, but only after rate control, because on their own they trigger reflex tachycardia that raises dP/dt. Surgery / TEVAR physically obliterates the false lumen or covers the entry tear. Opioids (fentanyl) blunt the sympathetic pain surge that drives up both HR and BP.
Stanford (A/B) and DeBakey (I/II/III) classification. Type A / DeBakey I–II involve the ascending aorta; Type B / DeBakey III begin distal to the left subclavian.

🗂️

Classification — the vocabulary that drives every decision

Two anatomic systems are named in the 2022 ACC/AHA guideline. Stanford is the one that changes management at the bedside: does it touch the ascending aorta or not?

SystemCategoryAnatomyImplication
StanfordType AInvolves the ascending aorta (any entry site / distal extent). ~60–65% of cases.Surgical emergency
Type BOriginates distal to the left subclavian; ascending NOT involved.Medical first (unless complicated)
DeBakeyIAscending → arch → descending (whole aorta).= Stanford A
IIConfined to ascending aorta only.= Stanford A
IIIOriginates descending aorta (IIIa above / IIIb below diaphragm).= Stanford B

Timing (classic scheme, still operative for prognosis): acute <14 days, subacute 14–90 days, chronic >90 days; the guideline adds a hyperacute <24 h label. The acute window is when mortality is highest and survivors stabilize.

Acute aortic syndrome (AAS) spectrumWhat it isManagement by location
Classic dissectionIntimal tear + true/false lumenA → surgery; B → medical vs TEVAR
Intramural hematoma (IMH)Hematoma in the media with no demonstrable intimal tear (~10% of AAS)Type A IMH → prompt surgery; Type B IMH → medical unless complicated
Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (PAU)Ulcer erodes through the internal elastic lamina into the mediaUrgent repair if rupture, ascending PAU + IMH, or refractory pain
Complicated Type B = any of: rupture / impending rupture, branch-vessel malperfusion (renal, mesenteric, limb, spinal), dissection extension, rapid aortic expansion, refractory pain, or refractory hypertension → intervene (TEVAR first-line). Otherwise it's uncomplicated → medical therapy. Consensus "high-risk" imaging features that predict progression even when uncomplicated include total aortic diameter >40 mm, false-lumen diameter >22 mm, entry tear on the lesser curvature, and bloody pleural effusion.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — IRAD frequency and the mechanism behind each

The classic teaching is "tearing chest pain radiating to the back" — but the registry data (IRAD, Hagan JAMA 2000, N=464) show dissection is a great mimic. The single most reliable feature is abrupt, maximal-at-onset severe pain; the "tearing" quality is present in only about half. Read each finding as a clue to where the tear has extended.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Any pain~96%Adventitial stretch + branch ischemia. Painless dissection (~6%) hides in diabetics, steroid users, and the elderly.
Abrupt onset (max at onset)~85%Instantaneous intimal tear — unlike the crescendo build of MI. The most discriminating single feature.
Severe / "worst ever"~91%Sudden maximal disruption of a richly innervated wall.
Chest pain (Type A ~79% > B ~63%)~73%Ascending/arch somatic + visceral afferents; anterior chest pain points to Type A (retrosternal ascending aorta).
Sharp quality~64%More common descriptor than "tearing." Quality alone cannot rule dissection in or out.
Back pain (Type B ~64% > A ~47%)~53%Descending aorta lies paravertebral/posterior → back pain flags Type B.
Tearing / ripping~51%The "classic" quality — but present in only half. Its absence does NOT exclude dissection.
New AR murmur (Type A ~44%)~32%Proximal dissection disrupts the valve annulus / prolapses a leaflet → acute aortic regurgitation. Diastolic decrescendo.
Abdominal pain (Type B ~43%)~30%Distal extension / mesenteric–renal malperfusion.
Migrating pain~17%Antegrade false-lumen propagation as the tear travels down the aorta.
Pulse deficit (Type A ~19% > B ~9%)~15%Flap/false lumen dynamically occludes a branch ostium. An SBP differential >20 mmHg between arms is the bedside equivalent.
Shock / tamponade (Type A ~13%)~8%Type A rupture into the pericardium, acute severe AR, or free rupture → the "hypotensive Type A" who is dying now.
Syncope (Type A ~13% > B ~4%)~9%Tamponade, arch-vessel/cerebral hypoperfusion, or rupture — a red flag for Type A even without pain.
CVA / focal neuro deficit~5%Carotid/arch-vessel dissection. Broader neuro deficits reach ~15–17% in some series.
Read the patternAnterior chest pain, a new AR murmur, syncope, hypotension, or a pulse deficit push you toward Type A (the surgical emergency). Back/abdominal pain with severe hypertension points toward Type B. But any abrupt max-at-onset pain in a patient with hypertension or aortopathy is dissection until an image says otherwise.
Contrast CT — Stanford Type A dissection: an intimal flap divides the true and false lumen in the ascending aorta.

Imaging findings — what to look for, and when it shows

FindingModality / frequencyWhy
Widened mediastinumCXR ~62%Blood/hematoma expands the aortic silhouette. Supportive, not diagnostic.
Abnormal aortic contour / knobCXR ~50%Distorted aortic outline from the dissected, dilated wall.
Normal chest x-ray~12%A clear film does not exclude dissection — image definitively if suspicion is real.
Intimal flap + true/false lumenCTA ~100% sensThe pathognomonic finding — a mobile flap separating two contrast columns. First-line in the stable patient.
Intimal flap / AR / effusionTEE ~98% sensBedside test for the unstable patient — no transport, no contrast; also grades AR and detects tamponade.
Pericardial effusion, dilated root, ARPOCUS/TTERules complications in (cannot rule out). A flap + effusion + new AR = Type A until proven otherwise.

🧪

Reading the labs & ECG — what each value is telling you

TestWhat it means & why it moves
D-dimerThe false lumen is a large clotting surface → D-dimer rises fast (sensitivity ~97%). Used as a rule-out only in combination: ADD-RS ≤1 + D-dimer <500 ng/mL → 0.3% miss (ADvISED). A positive D-dimer is nonspecific (PE, sepsis, age). Never use it as a standalone rule-in.
TroponinElevated in ~25% — from coronary ostial dissection (usually RCA) or demand ischemia. A positive troponin does NOT exclude dissection; this is exactly the trap that leads to lethal heparin/thrombolysis in a misread "NSTEMI."
ECGNormal in ~31%; nonspecific ST/T changes ~41%; LVH ~26%. A true inferior STEMI pattern (~3%) from RCA ostial involvement is the dangerous mimic — pain radiating to the back + STEMI should make you look at the root before the cath lab.
CreatinineRises with renal malperfusion (dynamic flap covering the renal ostium or static extension). Also gates contrast and nitroprusside (thiocyanate) decisions.
LactateRising lactate = mesenteric or limb malperfusion — a marker that an uncomplicated Type B has become complicated and needs intervention.
HemoglobinA falling Hgb signals slow rupture / hemothorax / hemopericardium. Type & cross early; keep blood available.
The three "reassuring" tests that fail to exclude dissection: a normal ECG (31%), a normal chest x-ray (12%), and a positive troponin (which points you at ACS). If the pain story fits, image the aorta — don't let a normal or misleading test talk you out of it.
🩺 Clinic — surveillance, BP control & genetic aortopathy
Assess

Who lands in your clinic

🔍

The outpatient dissection population

Acute dissection is an ED/ICU event — but a great deal of aortic disease lives in clinic, and getting it right prevents the catastrophe:

  • Post-dissection / post-repair survivors on lifelong surveillance and blood-pressure control — the residual (chronic) false lumen can grow for years.
  • Genetic aortopathy — Marfan (FBN1), Loeys-Dietz (TGFBR1/2), vascular Ehlers-Danlos (COL3A1), familial thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection (ACTA2), bicuspid aortic valve, Turner syndrome — plus their first-degree relatives.
  • Known thoracic aortic aneurysm approaching a repair threshold.
  • Uncontrolled hypertension — the dominant modifiable risk factor (~72% of dissections have a hypertension history).
Risk factorWhy it matters
Chronic hypertensionSupplies the shear stress that drives medial degeneration and the tear. Single biggest lever you control.
Marfan / Loeys-Dietz / vEDSGenetically weak media → dissection at younger age and smaller diameters; need lower repair thresholds and lifelong follow-up.
Bicuspid aortic valveAssociated ascending aneurysm and aortopathy independent of valve function.
Prior aneurysm / prior dissectionMarks established aortic disease; residual false lumen can re-dissect or expand.
Cocaine / methamphetamine, heavy weightliftingTransient extreme dP/dt surges; counsel avoidance.
The index dissection patient is often the sentinel for a familial disease — every new aortopathy diagnosis should trigger a conversation about screening first-degree relatives.
Workup

Surveillance & screening — what to order & when

🖥️

Imaging & genetic workup

CT or MRA (post-dissection)2022 ACC/AHA Class I surveillance after any dissection (repaired or medical): at 1 month, 6 months, 12 months, then annually if stable. Watch total diameter and false-lumen status.Serial
TTE (screening)First-line to screen first-degree relatives of a patient with root/ascending aneurysm or dissection, and to follow bicuspid valve + root/ascending diameter. Use CT/MRI if TTE is incomplete or the arch/descending aorta must be seen.Screen
Genetic testing + counselingOffer to syndromic features, a positive family history, or early onset (<60 yr). If a pathogenic variant is found → cascade testing of relatives.If indicated
BP log / home monitoringEvery visit — the modifiable driver. Target <130/80. Confirm with out-of-office readings.Every visit
BMP, lipids, HbA1cRenal function before ACEi/ARB; global cardiovascular risk (statin, diabetes) — atherosclerosis accelerates aortic disease.Baseline
Match the imaging modality to the patient: MRA (no ionizing radiation, no iodinated contrast) is preferred for young patients and pregnancy needing repeated surveillance; CT is faster and better for the acute/pre-operative map. Keep the modality and technique consistent so diameter measurements are comparable over time.
Treat

Chronic medical therapy — first-line → escalation

💊

The goal: BP <130/80 with dP/dt-lowering therapy anchored on a β-blocker

2022 ACC/AHA Class I

Chronic therapy has two jobs: keep BP <130/80 mmHg and keep dP/dt low so a residual or at-risk aorta stops growing. The β-blocker does both and is the anchor; add an ARB (especially in Marfan) and then other agents to reach goal.

1
β-blocker — the anchor (lowers dP/dt)
Reduces the force & rate of each ejection, not just the pressure
▾
β-blockade lowers heart rate and contractility, cutting dP/dt — the wedge force that propagates a dissection. IRAD data show long-term β-blockers improve survival (especially after Type A), so this class is continued lifelong.
DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxIf intolerant / notes
Metoprolol succinate25–50 mg dailydouble q1–2 wk as HR/BP allowup to 200 mg dailyCardioselective — safe in COPD/asthma. Tartrate 25–100 mg BID is the twice-daily form.
Bisoprolol2.5–5 mg dailyincrease q1–2 wk10 mg dailyHighly β1-selective; once daily.
Carvedilol6.25 mg BIDdouble q2 wk25 mg BIDCombined α/β — extra BP effect; good if hypertension is hard to control.
Atenolol25–50 mg dailyq1–2 wk100 mg dailyCommon in Marfan trials; avoid in significant CKD (renally cleared).
Target resting HR <60–70 as tolerated — the rate matters as much as the pressure. If a β-blocker is truly contraindicated (severe reactive airway disease, high-grade AV block), use a non-dihydropyridine CCB — verapamil 180–480 mg/day or diltiazem 120–360 mg/day — which also lowers HR and dP/dt.
2
Add an ARB (or ACE inhibitor)
Especially Marfan — slows aortic-root growth
▾
Angiotensin-receptor blockade lowers wall stress and, in Marfan, antagonizes TGF-β signaling that drives medial degeneration. Trial evidence (COMPARE, AIMS, and a 1,442-patient IPD meta-analysis) shows ARBs roughly halve the root-growth rate, additive to a β-blocker.
DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxIf allergic / intolerant
Losartan50 mg dailyincrease q2–4 wk; recheck BMP100 mg dailyBest-studied in Marfan. Cough is an ACEi problem, not ARB.
Irbesartan150 mg dailyq2–4 wk300 mg dailyAIMS-trial agent.
Lisinopril (ACEi alt)10 mg dailyq2–4 wk40 mg dailyIf ARB unavailable. ACEi + ARB together is not used. Angioedema → switch class.
ACEi/ARBs are teratogenic — stop and switch (usually to labetalol) before or as soon as pregnancy is planned/confirmed.
3
Add-on antihypertensives to reach <130/80
Layer agents; then consider elective repair
▾
DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxNotes
Amlodipine (DHP CCB)5 mg dailyq2–4 wk10 mg dailyPure vasodilator — fine here because the β-blocker already controls reflex tachycardia. Ankle edema is dose-related.
Chlorthalidone / HCTZ12.5–25 mg dailyq2–4 wk25 mg dailyThiazide add-on; watch K⁺/Na⁺.
Spironolactone25 mg dailyas needed50 mg dailyFor resistant hypertension; monitor K⁺.

Then think surgery: refer for elective repair once diameter or growth crosses threshold (see the monitoring section) — the medical regimen buys time, it does not cure the aneurysm.

Avoid isolated hydralazine or minoxidil in aortopathy — direct vasodilators without adequate β-blockade provoke reflex tachycardia that raises dP/dt.
Monitor

Surveillance cadence & repair thresholds

📈

What to recheck, when, and when to refer for surgery

  • After a dissection (repaired or medical): CT/MRA at 1, 6, and 12 months, then annually if stable (Class I). Bring it forward for new pain, new malperfusion, or a growing false lumen.
  • Aneurysm surveillance (no dissection): interval scaled to size and etiology — roughly annual, or every 6 months as diameter nears threshold or in aggressive genotypes.
  • After starting/uptitrating ACEi/ARB: BMP (K⁺, Cr) at 1–2 weeks.
  • Every visit: BP (target <130/80), resting HR (target <60–70), symptom review, medication adherence.

Elective repair thresholds (2022 ACC/AHA — ascending/root)

PopulationDiameter thresholdGrowth threshold
Sporadic degenerative aneurysm≥5.5 cm (5.0 cm at experienced multidisciplinary centers)≥0.5 cm/yr, or ≥0.3 cm/yr over 2 yr
Marfan syndrome≥5.0 cm (4.5 cm at experienced centers)≥0.3 cm/yr
Loeys-Dietz syndrome~4.5 cm, gene-dependent (lower for high-risk TGFBR variants)≥0.3 cm/yr
Bicuspid aortic valve≥5.5 cm (5.0 cm with risk factors / at experienced centers)≥0.3 cm/yr
Thresholds fall for shorter patients (index diameter to height/BSA), a strong family history of early dissection, or before pregnancy — an experienced aortic center individualizes the number. Growth rate can trump absolute size.

Activity & pregnancy counseling

  • Activity: avoid heavy isometric/resistance training, maximal Valsalva, and intense competitive/collision sports; moderate aerobic exercise is encouraged (commonly framed as staying below ~50% of maximal effort — consensus phrasing, not a hard number).
  • Pregnancy: counsel risk when the root/ascending aorta is ≥4.0 cm; pre-pregnancy repair for Marfan root >4.5 cm (and consider at 4.0–4.5 cm with risk factors). Delivery mode by size: <4.0 cm vaginal, 4.0–4.5 cm individualized, ≥4.5 cm or chronic dissection → cesarean.
Comorbidities

How comorbidities change management

🔗

The company aortic disease keeps

ComorbidityHow it interactsWhat changes
CKDIodinated contrast risk; nitroprusside → thiocyanate accumulation.Weigh contrast against life-threat (usually still image); prefer MRA for surveillance; avoid prolonged nitroprusside — use nicardipine/clevidipine + esmolol.
PregnancyPeripartum hemodynamic/hormonal stress; connective-tissue disease amplifies risk.β-blocker of choice = labetalol (or metoprolol); avoid ACEi/ARB (teratogenic) and nitroprusside (fetal cyanide); MRI without gadolinium.
COPD / asthmaReflex fear of β-blockade; bronchospasm risk.Use cardioselective agents (metoprolol, bisoprolol); in the ICU favor esmolol (β1-selective, 9-min half-life → reversible).
Bradycardia / high-grade AV blockβ-blockers may be unsafe.Use a rate-sparing vasodilator ± temporary pacing to still permit anti-impulse therapy.
Severe acute AR (Type A)Compensatory tachycardia partly protects cardiac output.Avoid excessive bradycardia; use β-blockade cautiously and expedite surgery.
Cocaine / methamphetamineSympathetic surge + coronary vasospasm.Benzodiazepines first to blunt central drive; labetalol (α+β) or diltiazem acceptable; phentolamine for refractory α-hypertension.
Marfan / Loeys-Dietz / BAVWeak media, earlier dissection.Lifelong surveillance, lower repair thresholds, ARB on board, genetics + family screening.
Prior cardiac surgeryPericardial adhesions.May limit tamponade but make redo sternotomy harder/higher-risk.
Drugs to avoid in aortopathy / dissection: fluoroquinolones (FDA warning, Dec 2018 — associated with aneurysm/dissection; avoid in known aortopathy or high-risk patients); isolated direct vasodilators (hydralazine, minoxidil, or nitroprusside without a β-blocker — reflex tachycardia ↑dP/dt); anticoagulants / antiplatelets / thrombolytics given for a misdiagnosed "MI" (catastrophic hemorrhage/tamponade); and stimulants / sympathomimetic decongestants (pseudoephedrine, cocaine).
Scores

Risk score — ADD-RS

🧮

Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS) — 0 to 3

ADD-RS (2010 AHA / IRAD, validated in ADvISED) scores one point per category if any item in that category is present. Use it to decide who needs immediate imaging and who can be ruled out with a D-dimer.

① High-risk conditions (+1 if any)
Marfan / connective-tissue disease · family hx aortic disease · known aortic valve disease · recent aortic manipulation · known thoracic aortic aneurysm +1
② High-risk pain (+1 if any)
Chest / back / abdominal pain that is abrupt in onset, severe in intensity, OR ripping / tearing +1
③ High-risk exam (+1 if any)
Pulse deficit / SBP differential · focal neuro deficit + pain · new AR murmur + pain · hypotension / shock +1
0
ADD-RS ≥2 → go straight to CTA (or TEE if unstable). ADD-RS ≤1 → check D-dimer; if <500 ng/mL, aortic workup can be stopped (ADvISED: 0.3% miss, spares ~50% of imaging). A D-dimer is not ordered when ADD-RS ≥2 — image instead.
ADD-RS ≥1 captures ~95% of confirmed dissections. The score is a rule-out aid, not a rule-in — a low score with a convincing story still warrants imaging.

Prevent

USPSTF A/B & whole-patient prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B screening for the vascular patient

GradeRecommendationPopulation
BOne-time AAA screening ultrasound — the abdominal-aorta analogue; aortopathy is frequently diffuseMen 65–75 y who have ever smoked
AHypertension screening (confirm out-of-office) — the dominant modifiable driverAll adults ≥18 y
ATobacco-cessation counseling + FDA-approved pharmacotherapyAll adults who use tobacco
BStatin for primary prevention of CVDAdults 40–75 y with ≥1 risk factor and 10-yr risk ≥10%
BHealthy-diet / physical-activity behavioral counselingAdults with CVD risk factors

Disease-specific prevention

  • Blood pressure <130/80 and resting HR <60–70 — the single biggest lever against dissection and re-dissection.
  • Screen first-degree relatives of every aortopathy/dissection index case (TTE ± genetic cascade testing).
  • Smoking cessation (accelerates aneurysm growth) and lipid/atherosclerosis control.
  • Avoid fluoroquinolones when another antibiotic will do (FDA 2018 aortic warning).
  • Counsel activity & pregnancy as above; make sure the patient knows the red-flag symptoms that mean "call 911, not the clinic."
Escalate

When to send to the ED now

🚑

Red flags → 911 / ED, not the next appointment

Any abrupt, severe, max-at-onset chest, back, or abdominal pain — especially "tearing/ripping," migrating, or with syncope — in a patient with hypertension or aortopathy. This is a call-911 event, not a clinic workup.
New neurologic deficit, cold/pulseless limb, SBP differential >20 mmHg between arms, a new diastolic (AR) murmur with pain, or hypotension/syncope → immediate ED for CTA. Do not give aspirin/heparin "just in case it's an MI" until dissection is excluded.
🛏️ Wards — subacute / uncomplicated Type B & post-op step-down
Admit

Who belongs on the floor

📋

Level-of-care reality check

Almost no acute dissection starts on a general ward. Every acute dissection — Type A awaiting/after surgery, and every acute Type B — is an ICU or step-down patient initially, on IV anti-impulse therapy with an arterial line. The floor is where they land after the acute phase:

  • Uncomplicated Type B transitioning from IV to oral therapy, pain-free, BP controlled, off drips, with stable serial imaging.
  • Post-operative / post-TEVAR patients stepped down from the ICU.
  • Subacute / chronic dissection admitted for BP optimization, symptom flare, or pre-operative workup.
If you are being asked to admit an acute dissection directly to a general medical floor, stop — it needs continuous arterial-line BP monitoring and titratable IV therapy. That is an ICU/step-down conversation.

Treat

IV → oral transition ladder

💊

Converting drips to a durable oral regimen

Goal on the floor: reproduce the ICU targets (HR <60–70, SBP <120, then BP <130/80) with oral agents so the patient is drip-free and dischargeable. Anchor on a β-blocker, layer on an ARB/ACEi and a CCB.

1
Oral β-blocker — the backbone
Overlap with the esmolol/labetalol drip before weaning it
▾
DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxNotes
Metoprolol tartrate25–50 mg PO BIDdouble q1–2 days on the floor as HR/BP allow100 mg BIDConvert to succinate once daily at the same total daily dose for discharge (50 mg BID tartrate → 100 mg succinate daily).
Labetalol PO100–200 mg PO BIDincrease q1–2 days200–400 mg BID–TID (max ~2,400 mg/day)Combined α/β — strong BP effect; useful when hypertension dominates or in pregnancy.
Carvedilol6.25 mg PO BIDdouble q2–3 days25 mg BIDAlternative combined α/β.
Overlap, don't gap: give the first oral β-blocker dose and let it take effect before weaning the IV drip, so dP/dt never rebounds. Don't wean the drip and "see how they do."
2
Add ARB/ACEi, then a dihydropyridine CCB
To reach BP <130/80
▾
DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxNotes
Losartan50 mg PO dailyq2–3 days; recheck BMP100 mg dailyRenoprotective; first add-on (esp. Marfan). Hold if AKI/hyperkalemia.
Amlodipine5 mg PO dailyq2–3 days10 mg dailyAdd once β-blockade is established (reflex tachycardia is covered).
Do not add hydralazine without adequate β-blockade — reflex tachycardia raises dP/dt. Avoid pure vasodilators as a "quick fix" for a floor BP spike.
Monitor

What to trend each day

📈

The daily ward checklist

  • BP in both arms + full pulse exam — a new differential or pulse deficit means extension/malperfusion.
  • Resting HR — is anti-impulse control holding on oral agents (target <60–70)?
  • Creatinine — renal malperfusion; also guides ARB dosing.
  • Hemoglobin — downtrend = bleeding/slow rupture.
  • Lactate — if any abdominal/limb concern.
  • Pain score — recurrent or refractory pain is the earliest sign the aorta is not quiet.
Escalate

When to call ICU / surgery

⬆️

Concrete escalation triggers

Move back to the ICU (and call surgery/vascular) for any of: recurrent or refractory pain; SBP not controllable on the oral regimen (or needing a drip again); new pulse deficit or neuro change; rising creatinine or lactate (malperfusion); falling hemoglobin (bleeding); or imaging showing aortic expansion / new complication.
Sudden severe chest/back pain with hypotension, syncope, or a widening mediastinum → treat as rupture / retrograde Type A: activate surgery, type & cross, and transfer emergently.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: SBP controlled <130 mmHg on the oral regimen for ~24 h, resting HR at goal, pain-free, stable serial imaging, no malperfusion, and a clear plan: surveillance CT/MRA at 1/6/12 months, cardiology/vascular follow-up, genetics referral, and BP self-monitoring with red-flag teaching.

Home

Independent, BP controlled on orals, reliable follow-up. Most uncomplicated Type B / post-step-down patients.

Home health

Home + nurse visits for BP checks / wound care after repair or TEVAR.

SNF

Needs 24h skilled nursing (deconditioning, complex meds), <3h therapy/day — common after prolonged Type A recovery.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines — e.g., post-op stroke or deconditioning with rehab potential.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (vent weaning, complications) >25 days after a difficult surgical course.

Hospice / palliative

Inoperable Type A or a patient declining surgery with limited prognosis — comfort-focused, goals-of-care led.
🫀 ICU — anti-impulse therapy, surgical triage & malperfusion
Admit

ICU triage & the acute algorithm

🚨

Every acute dissection is an ICU patient — then anatomy decides

All acute dissections need the unit: continuous arterial-line BP, titratable IV anti-impulse therapy, and immediate access to surgery. The first fork is anatomic — Type A goes to the OR now; Type B is medical unless complicated. Start anti-impulse therapy while the surgeon is being called; don't wait.

Diagnostic & management algorithm: risk-stratify with ADD-RS + D-dimer, image with CTA (or bedside TEE if unstable), then split acute care by anatomy — Type A to emergent surgery, Type B by complicated vs uncomplicated.
Type A = surgical emergency. Untreated it kills ~1–2%/hour early (contemporary IRAD ~0.12%/hr once pathways engage); medical mortality ~58% vs surgical ~17–26%. The job of medicine here is to lower dP/dt and get the patient to the OR alive — not to "stabilize and admit."
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, targets, and the things that kill quietly

  • Arterial line in the arm with the higher / least-affected pressure — measure BP in all four limbs at baseline so you don't chase a pseudohypotension from a malperfused limb.
  • Two large-bore IVs, type & crossmatch, keep blood available — this patient can rupture.
  • Targets: HR 60–80 bpm first, then SBP <120 mmHg (or the lowest that preserves cerebral, coronary, renal, and spinal perfusion). Follow urine output, mentation, and lactate as perfusion read-outs.
  • Foley for urine output (renal malperfusion / resuscitation marker); serial neuro checks and pulse exams.
  • Continuous ECG — watch for the inferior-STEMI pattern of RCA ostial involvement.
No anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or thrombolytics. If this was mistaken for ACS and heparin/lytics were given, expect catastrophic bleeding into the false lumen/pericardium. Withhold and reassess the instant dissection is on the differential.
Support

Anti-impulse therapy — the drips & doses

💉

Rate control FIRST, then vasodilate — never the reverse

HR 60–80 → SBP <120
The order is physiologic law. A β-blocker cuts dP/dt (force × rate) — the wedge that propagates the tear. A vasodilator given first drops afterload, the baroreflex fires, heart rate and ejection velocity climb, and dP/dt rises even as the pressure falls — accelerating the dissection. So: get HR to 60–80, then add a vasodilator for any residual SBP >120. Give fentanyl 25–100 mcg IV for pain, which blunts the sympathetic surge driving both.

Step 1 — IV β-blocker (rate control, give first)

DrugStart / loadTitrationMaxWhy pick it
Esmolol500 mcg/kg IV load over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min infusion+50 mcg/kg/min q4–5 min200 mcg/kg/min (up to 300)Ultra-short half-life (~9 min), RBC-esterase metabolism → ideal in COPD/asthma, labile patients, or if surgery is imminent (turns off fast).
Labetalol20 mg IV over 2 min20–80 mg IV q10 min, OR 0.5–2 mg/min infusion300 mg cumulative (bolus); ~10 mg/min infusionCombined α/β → lowers HR and BP in one agent; a common single-drug choice.
Metoprolol5 mg IV q5 min ×3 (max 15 mg)then 5 mg IV q4–6h PRN—Rate control with less BP drop; useful bridge to oral.
β-blocker contraindicated? (severe bronchospasm, high-grade AV block) — use a non-dihydropyridine CCB for rate/dP/dt control: diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 min then 5–20 mg/h, or verapamil IV. Do not skip straight to a pure vasodilator.

Step 2 — IV vasodilator (only after HR <80)

AgentMechanismStart → titration → maxEffectCaution
NicardipineDHP CCB (arterial)5 mg/h → +2.5 mg/h q5–15 min → 15 mg/hSmooth SBP reduction; preserves cerebral flowEasy to titrate; no cyanide risk. Preferred in CKD.
ClevidipineDHP CCB, ultra-short (arterial)1–2 mg/h → double q90 s, finer near goal → ~21 mg/h (lipid cap; 32 mg/h theoretical)Rapid, precise SBP control; seconds-fast offLipid emulsion — avoid in egg/soy allergy, severe hypertriglyceridemia.
NitroprussideArterial + venous NO donor0.3–0.5 mcg/kg/min → titrate → 10 mcg/kg/minPotent, immediate BP dropNEVER without a β-blocker (reflex tachycardia ↑dP/dt). Cyanide with >2 mcg/kg/min prolonged; thiocyanate in renal failure. Limit duration/dose.

The hypotensive Type A — a different problem

AgentReceptorsDoseEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 > β10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑SVR, restores MAP ~65Hypotensive/shock Type A — presume tamponade, acute AR, or rupture. Judicious fluids + NE while racing to the OR.
Resist routine pericardiocentesis in tamponade from Type A. Decompressing the pericardium re-accelerates bleeding into the low-pressure space and can precipitate arrest. If peri-arrest and the OR is unreachable, drain only small controlled aliquots to restore a minimally acceptable perfusion pressure as a bridge — the definitive fix is the operating room.
Definitive

Surgery & endovascular repair

🔧

Who gets the OR, who gets a stent, who stays medical

ScenarioDefinitive treatmentDetail
Type A (any)Emergent open repairReplace ascending ± hemiarch, open distal anastomosis under hypothermic circulatory arrest ± cerebral perfusion. Valve: resuspend if leaflets intact; root replacement (Bentall or valve-sparing David) for root aneurysm/genetic aortopathy. Operate even with malperfusion.
Uncomplicated Type BMedical (ICU)Anti-impulse therapy + serial imaging (Class I). Preemptive TEVAR improves late (5-yr) aorta-specific survival (INSTEAD-XL) and may be offered to high-risk features.
Complicated Type BTEVAR first-lineCover the primary entry tear; secure proximal/distal landing zones; left subclavian often covered → revascularize. Malperfusion may also need branch stenting/fenestration.

TEVAR complications to anticipate: retrograde Type A dissection (~1.3–3%, high mortality), spinal cord ischemia (~3–12% — mitigate with CSF drainage and MAP support), and endoleak (types I/III most concerning). Balance these against the malperfusion/rupture risk that drove the intervention.
Rescue

Malperfusion & spinal-cord protection

⚙️

The complications that need a procedure, not more drip

  • Malperfusion — know the two mechanisms. Dynamic (~80%): the mobile flap intermittently covers a branch ostium (pressure/position-dependent) → relieved by restoring true-lumen flow (TEVAR / fenestration). Static: the dissection extends into the branch itself (fixed narrowing/thrombosis) → needs branch stenting or bypass. Rising creatinine, lactate, a cold limb, or paraplegia are the tells.
  • Spinal cord ischemia (esp. extensive TEVAR): place a CSF (lumbar) drain targeting CSF pressure ~≤10 mmHg (commonly cited 8–12 mmHg), and support MAP (often ≥85–90 mmHg) to keep spinal cord perfusion = MAP − CSF pressure adequate. Reverse a new deficit urgently with drainage + pressure augmentation.
  • Acute severe AR / tamponade / rupture (Type A): the definitive rescue is the OR — see the anti-impulse and hypotensive-Type-A guidance above.
New or worsening malperfusion converts an "uncomplicated Type B" into a complicated one → call vascular/surgery for TEVAR ± branch intervention. Medical therapy alone will not reopen a malperfused bed.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to step-down / floor

Downgrade when all hold: HR and SBP at goal on oral agents (off all drips) for ~24 h; no malperfusion (stable creatinine/lactate, intact pulses and neuro exam); stable serial imaging; pain-free; and hemoglobin stable.
Not yet if… the patient still needs any IV titratable agent to hold SBP <120, has recurrent pain, a rising creatinine/lactate, a downtrending hemoglobin, or imaging showing expansion — those belong in the unit. A quiet number on a drip is not "stable."

ICU disposition beyond the floor: an inoperable Type A or a patient declining surgery is a goals-of-care / palliative conversation; a prolonged complicated post-op course may route through LTAC (see the Wards disposition grid).

Pearls

Clinical pearls & prognosis

💡

The 14 things that catch dissection — or get it missed

  1. Pain out of proportion + normal ECG + a hypertension history = think dissection BEFORE you give heparin for "NSTEMI." Anticoagulation or thrombolysis in an unrecognized dissection is lethal.
  2. Check BP in both arms. An SBP differential >20 mmHg or a pulse deficit is a branch-vessel red flag.
  3. A positive troponin does NOT exclude dissection — ~25% have elevated troponin from coronary ostial involvement or demand. It's the classic route to a fatal misdiagnosis.
  4. D-dimer <500 + ADD-RS ≤1 rules out AAS (~0.3% miss, ADvISED) — but a positive D-dimer is nonspecific and never rules dissection in.
  5. Painless dissection (~6%) hides in diabetics, steroid users, and the elderly; syncope may be the only clue — and syncope points to Type A.
  6. New diastolic (AR) murmur + chest pain = Type A until proven otherwise (AR present in ~44% of Type A).
  7. Inferior STEMI + tearing pain radiating to the back → look at the aortic root before the cath lab or lytics (RCA ostial dissection).
  8. Young, tall patient with sudden "pleuritic" chest pain and a Marfan habitus — think dissection, not just pneumothorax.
  9. Rate control BEFORE vasodilation, always. A vasodilator first raises dP/dt via reflex tachycardia and extends the tear.
  10. A normal CXR (~12%) and a normal ECG (~31%) do NOT exclude dissection — if the story fits, image the aorta.
  11. In hypotensive Type A, resist pericardiocentesis — decompression re-accelerates bleeding; go to the OR (small controlled aliquots only if peri-arrest).
  12. Long-term β-blockers improve survival (IRAD, especially Type A) — continue them lifelong.
  13. Partial false-lumen thrombosis predicts LATE death (2.7× vs a patent lumen) — it drives how intensively you follow the aorta.
  14. Avoid fluoroquinolones in aortopathy (FDA 2018) and screen first-degree relatives — the index case is often the sentinel for a familial disease.

Prognosis by the numbers

MetricValue
Overall in-hospital mortality (IRAD)~27%
Type A — surgical vs medical mortality~17–26% vs ~58%
Untreated Type A hourly mortality (early)classic ~1–2%/hr; contemporary IRAD ~0.12%/hr
Type B — medical in-hospital mortality~10–14%
Surgical Type A 30-day (GERAADA registry)~16.9%
False-lumen prognosispartial thrombosis → 2.7× mortality vs patent
the whole disease is a race between two clocks — the tear peeling the aorta apart, and your team lowering dP/dt and getting a Type A to the OR. Every β-blocker milligram and every minute saved is time bought on the first clock.
